Empirical Research Plan: Boston’s 1872 Fire, Re-building, and Cross-Property Spillovers  

======================================================================  

1. Identification Strategy  
----------------------------------------------------------------------
Preferred approach: Plot–level Difference-in-Differences with an event-study (dynamic DID) extension.

• Why DID?  
  – We observe the same individual plots repeatedly before and after an unexpected, one-off disaster that struck only part of the downtown area.  
  – Treated plots (burned) and nearby never-burned plots were subject to the same city‐wide demand, macro conditions, finance, and tax assessment rules; the only sharp difference is that one subset was forced to tear down and rebuild.  
  – DID exploits that “as-if random” spatial variation in destruction to recover the causal effect on land values and can be extended to measure spillovers on plots at increasing distance.  

• Alternative designs considered  
  – RDD (distance to burn boundary) is tempting but the boundary was not drawn by officials ex-ante; wind direction and fire-fighting effort produced a ragged frontier that is plausibly quasi-random but the small number of plots right at the edge makes precision difficult.  
  – IV (using wind direction or water-pipe diameter to predict destruction) could complement DID robustness checks, but the baseline two-way-fixed-effects DID is simpler and transparent given balanced pre-fire data.  

2. Treatment and Control  
----------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
  TREATED_i = 1 if plot i’s primary structure was destroyed in the November 1872 conflagration; 0 otherwise.

Control group  
  – Preferred: plots inside the tax-assessment sample that were never reported as destroyed in 1872 (or any major fire 1866-1874) and lie within a pre-specified “downtown business district” ring (say, within 1 km of Boston’s Old State House).  
  – For spillover estimates, we will further split untreated plots by distance bands from the burn perimeter:  
      0–100 m, 100–250 m, 250–500 m, >500 m.  
  – Plots in other post-1872 fire footprints are dropped to avoid contamination.  

Treatment timing  
  POST_t = 1 for assessment years ≥ 1873 (first tax roll after the fire); 0 for 1867, 1869, 1871.  
  – 1872 assessments refer to January 1, 1872 and therefore precede the November blaze; they are coded as pre-treatment.  

3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
----------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel pre-trends: In the absence of the fire, assessed land values of treated and control plots would have followed the same trajectory.  
  – Plausibility: Both groups shared the same commercial environment, municipal services, and were assessed by the same officials. Multiple pre-fire years allow an empirical test.  

A2. No anticipatory behavior: Owners could not foresee the 1872 inferno in 1867-71 and adjust investment or petitions accordingly.  
  – Large accidental fires were common but timing/location was unanticipated; no insurance records indicate ex-ante demolition plans.  

A3. Stable composition and measurement: The identity of a “plot” (parcel footprint) is stable; assessment methods did not change discontinuously only for the burned area.  
  – The assessor’s handbook remained the same; we will verify that parcel IDs are consistent across years.  

A4. No differential contemporaneous shocks: Other policy changes affecting land value (e.g., road widening) were modest and city-wide.  
  – The only localised post-fire public work (Post Office Square) will be controlled for with a dummy.  

A5. Limited interference for baseline DID: Outcomes on a control plot should not be directly changed by the treatment status of its neighbor.  
  – Clearly violated if we study spillovers; but for the “own-plot” effect we will drop the inner 100 m ring from the control group. Spillovers are studied separately.  

4. Threats to Identification and Mitigation  
----------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Non-parallel pre-trends  
  – Diagnose with an event-study plot using only pre-years.  
  – If slopes differ, re-weight controls via entropy balancing on 1867–71 trends, or include parcel-specific linear time trends.  

T2. Spatially correlated shocks unrelated to fire (e.g., district-specific infrastructure upgrades)  
  – Control for time-varying road width, water-pipe diameter, and ward-year fixed effects.  
  – Show results hold when restricting to a narrow ring (e.g., ≤ 500 m from burn perimeter) so both treated and control plots share any local upgrades.  

T3. Selective post-fire reassessment bias  
  – Use Registry-of-Deeds transaction prices to proxy market value and confirm assessment ratios do not change differentially.  
  – Run regressions with deed prices (where available) as outcome.  
  – Instrument assessed value with lagged deed price to test robustness.  

5. R Code Outline (executable)  
----------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
# -------------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)     # fast data wrangling
library(fixest)         # regressions with fixed effects
library(ggplot2)        # plots
library(EValue)         # sensitivity
# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Load Data
# -------------------------------------------------------------------
assess  <- fread("boston_parcel_panel.csv")   # main dataset
distance<- fread("distance_to_burn_perimeter.csv") # distances

data <- merge(assess, distance, by = "plot_id")

# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Variable Construction
# -------------------------------------------------------------------
data[, treated := as.integer(burned1872 == 1)]
data[, post    := as.integer(year >= 1873)]
data[, ln_land_value := log(land_value_1872dollars)]

# Spillover groups
data[, dist_band :=
      cut(distance_m,
          breaks = c(-Inf,100,250,500,Inf),
          labels = c("00_100","100_250","250_500","gt500"))]

# Core sample: keep plots within 1km of State House and no other major fires
core <- data[within_1km == 1 & majorfire_1866_1874 == 0]

# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Main DID
# -------------------------------------------------------------------
did_mod <- feols(ln_land_value ~ treated*post | plot_id + year,
                 data = core, cluster = ~block_id)

etable(did_mod)

# Dynamic event study (reference = 1871)
core[, rel_year := year - 1872]
es_mod <- feols(ln_land_value ~ i(rel_year, treated, ref = -1) |
                plot_id + year, data = core, cluster = ~block_id)

iplot(es_mod)

# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Spillover regression (untreated only)
# -------------------------------------------------------------------
spill <- core[treated == 0]
spill_mod <- feols(ln_land_value ~ i(post, dist_band, ref = "gt500") |
                   plot_id + year, data = spill, cluster = ~block_id)
etable(spill_mod)

# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Robustness: entropy-balanced weights on pre-trends
# -------------------------------------------------------------------
library(ebal)
# Construct balancing
bal <- ebalance(Treatment = core$treated,
                X = as.matrix(core[, .(ln_land_value_lag1, ln_land_value_lag2)]))

core[, w := 1]
core[treated == 1, w := bal$w]
did_rb <- feols(ln_land_value ~ treated*post | plot_id + year,
                data = core, weights = ~w, cluster = ~block_id)
etable(list(Base = did_mod, EntBal = did_rb))
```

6. Expected Results  
----------------------------------------------------------------------
Economic theory (urban land-use models with indivisible structures) predicts that when replacement costs are partly covered by insurance and external capital, landowners will rebuild higher-quality premises that better match latent demand. Hence:  

• Own-plot effect: log land value should jump upward. A 10–15 percent increase (≈ 0.10–0.14 log points) relative to pre-fire trend seems plausible, equivalent to roughly half the annual growth Boston experienced in the previous two decades compressed into a single year.  

• Spillovers: Adjacent but unburned plots should also rise in value, but less: perhaps 3–6 percent within 100 m, decaying with distance and becoming negligible beyond 500 m.  

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (Difference-in-Differences)  
----------------------------------------------------------------------
C1: Common pre-fire trends visually flat and statistically indistinguishable ………………… 1  
C2: No anticipatory behavior (accidental fire) ……………………………………………………………… 1  
C3: No concurrent shocks differentially hitting treatment vs control …………………………… 0.5  
C4: No interference within core sample (after excluding inner buffer) ………………………… 0.5  
C5: Stable treatment assignment and measurement over time ……………………………………… 1  

Total = 4/5. The main residual concerns are spatial spillovers and any unobserved local policy changes. With robustness exercises (buffer exclusion, narrow rings, covariates, weighted trends), confidence in causal interpretation is high.
